title: GAUGE: A Formal Framework for Measuring Cryptographic Security under Heterogeneous Adversary Cost Models
abstract: Standards bodies report cryptographic security as a single number of bits, but this value depends on the adversary cost model used to price time, memory, and quantum resources. Different conventions can therefore produce different rankings of cryptographic schemes. GAUGE represents security as a function over admissible cost models, called a security profile. Comparisons then become comparisons between profiles, and ranking reversals become an explicit structural property rather than a measurement error.   We formalize price functionals over a cone of adversary cost models, show that security profiles are piecewise-linear and concave, and prove a rating trilemma: when two profiles cross, no rating can simultaneously be faithful to underlying costs, total over comparable pairs, and independent of the chosen cost model. We provide a polynomial-time linear-programming procedure that certifies whether the ranking of two schemes is robust, reverses under admissible models, or is genuinely incomparable.   We extend GAUGE with a two-layer risk measure combining stochastic cryptanalytic decay with uncertainty over the appropriate cost model. We evaluate the framework on NIST post-quantum standards, classical anchors, and a 25-year chronology of cryptanalytic breaks. The analysis certifies a ranking reversal for ML-KEM-512 versus AES-128 from a 4-5% shift in memory pricing, and measures a lattice-sieving cost drift of 9.79 bits per year over eight years. A hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-768 handshake reduces combined-break probability twenty-fold at a 2.3 kilobyte cost. The artifact reproduces all tables and figures in under seven seconds. GAUGE provides an explicit and auditable framework for reporting cryptographic security under competing cost models.
summary: This paper introduces GAUGE, a formal framework to measure cryptographic security not by a single bit-count, but by a 'security profile' that maps across all possible adversary cost models. It mathematically proves that different cost models can lead to contradictory security rankings, providing an explicit, auditable method to quantify this model dependence. This is crucial for standards bodies to report security honestly when underlying assumptions about attacker resources are uncertain.
main_problem: Current cryptographic security reporting relies on a single scalar bit-strength number, which is misleading because it depends entirely on the unstated adversary cost model used for pricing resources like time and memory.
main_result: The authors introduce GAUGE, a framework that models security as a 'security profile' (a function over all admissible cost models), proving that ranking reversals are structural properties rather than measurement errors.
method: The framework formalizes price functionals over a cone of cost models, proving that security profiles are piecewise-linear and concave, and uses linear programming to certify the robustness of security rankings.
model_or_system: The model is abstract, dealing with cryptographic schemes and the space of admissible adversary cost models ($\kappa$). It defines security as a function of these models, leading to the concept of a 'security profile' $S_K(\kappa)$.
key_observables: Security profile, Rating Trilemma, Robust/Reversing/Incomparable ranking status, Lattice-sieving cost drift (e.g., 9.79 bits/year).
important_parameters: Adversary cost model parameters (time, memory, quantum resources); time horizons ($	au$); decay rates ($\delta$); and the structure of the cost cone.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes the existence of a cone of admissible cost models and uses concepts like anchor-relative profiles to normalize comparisons.
figures_summary: Figure 1 conceptually maps cost models to security profiles; Table 1 compares schemes under multiple cost models, showing varying relative security costs.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem with scalar reporting, introduces the GAUGE profile framework, proves mathematical properties (concavity, linearity), develops the linear-programming certification procedure, and concludes with concrete evaluations on PQC standards and risk measures.
why_interesting: While not directly about physical quantum systems, the rigorous mathematical framework for uncertainty quantification and model dependence (risk measures, profile analysis) is highly relevant to any field where underlying assumptions or measurement models introduce systematic, non-Gaussian uncertainty.
